summary:
Yemen's Penal Code 1994 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Article 264 defines homosexuality between men as anal penetration and punishes unmarried participants with 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment, with a different penalty prescribed where the participants are married. Readings of the statute that treat the conduct as a capital offence circulate alongside the codified sentence, and a visitor should treat execution as a live risk rather than a remote theoretical maximum.

The statute's reach is territorial. Cairo 52's country review records that the penal provisions apply only in government-controlled regions, while the rest of the country sits under competing faction authorities, so legal exposure shifts at front lines and checkpoints. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 makes the same finding for events of 2025, describing Houthi and government factional control as determining where the law applies at all.

Where Houthi-run courts have applied the provisions, the sentences have been severe. Amnesty International documented more than 40 people sentenced to death, flogging or prison over same-sex conduct in January and February 2024: the Dhamar criminal court on 23 January sentenced nine to death, seven by stoning and two by crucifixion, with 23 others receiving six months to ten years for "homosexuality" or "spreading immorality", and an Ibb court on 1 February handed further death sentences. Amnesty demanded an immediate halt to the executions.

Formal law is only part of the exposure. Cairo 52 reports that the erosion of the rule of law, the humanitarian crisis and the growing power of militias have produced de facto criminalisation that is rarely enforced by any court but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands. Vigilante violence therefore operates outside any judicial process, and in neither setting does a visitor have a safe authority to appeal to.

Expression is constrained as well. Human Rights Watch's 2018 regional report identifies "breach of modesty" laws used against sexual and gender expression, and could find no activists in Yemen willing to speak about their work, a documented gap in whatever protection machinery the country retains.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026 places the sexual-orientation provisions inside the world's worst humanitarian crisis, with 19.5 million people needing aid. Consular capacity, medical evacuation and reliable movement are all shaped by that collapse, and none of it improves the position of a trans traveller caught up in a legal or vigilante process.

Yemen is one of 14 countries covered by Human Rights Watch's 2018 report in which zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and explicitly prohibit same-sex acts, which places the Yemeni regime within a wider regional pattern of morality-based criminal law rather than an isolated statute.

IPS reported from Sana'a in August 2013 that discretionary social enforcement sits on top of the statutory penalty: a gay man described hiding his long hair under a hood as "still problematic", and the account shows a conservative society enforcing conformity long before any court is involved.
localsOnly:
Residents of Houthi-controlled areas are subject to the faction's own moral-policing apparatus rather than to the ordinary courts, and it is these Houthi-run courts that handed the death and flogging sentences recorded by Amnesty International in early 2024. Residents in government-controlled regions face the Penal Code as written, with Article 264's distinction between married and unmarried participants determining whether the penalty is 100 lashes and up to a year or something else.

The social climate documented in Sana'a falls hardest on residents, who cannot leave. Conservative expectations govern dress, hair and public presentation, and concealment is described as a daily necessity rather than a precaution taken at a border.
outOfScopeNotes:
How the death-penalty readings of Article 264 relate to the codified sentence of 100 lashes and one year's imprisonment is unresolved in the sources available here; the statute text cited by GayLawNet does not itself specify a capital penalty, while Cairo 52 and IPS both report death as a possible outcome. The provision applicable where participants are married is likewise stated only as "differently prescribed" and has not been sourced in full.

No sourced material in this inventory addresses entry or visa screening, gender markers on passports or identity documents, recognition of a visitor's stated gender, or access to gender-affirming care in Yemen. These remain not sourced rather than cleared.

The frequency of enforcement outside the documented court cases and the current status of the 2024 death sentences, including whether any were carried out, are not established by the inventory.
